verdict: Leaning reject on the claims/statistics track, not because any individual arithmetic is wrong (the Wilson CIs, McNemar tests, and 16.7x/26.8x ratios check out) but because the keystone's central contrast — adapter vs. in-prompt delivery under a token budget — is run against an in-prompt baseline that is not the strongest available design, and because the abstract states several results (the objective contrast, the ceiling parity, the LiveCodeBench superset) more strongly than the body's own hedges support. The cross-file identifier-recovery result is real and the paired McNemar p=3.0e-6 against the floor is solid, but 'delivers context at parity with full-context prompting, at 16.7x fewer tokens' is not yet established against the honest in-prompt competitor, and the paper's own literature citation (RepoBench's own placement ablation) undercuts the fairness of the a2_clamp arm as currently constructed. The paper is unusually well-instrumented with self-critique (mutated-spec control, naive-dump null, sign-test caveats, escalate-mode structural note) — the authors clearly know where the soft spots are — but several of the fixes promised in review_response_v10 (fresh-pool re-estimate, explicit 'design property not evidence' framing for zero regressions, SHA-256 publication) remain open TODOs inside the submitted v13 text, and the abstract has not been reconciled with the more careful hedging in the body.

findings.location: §4 Setup / Table `tab:arms` ('The four-arm budgeted design', around 'a2_clamp, the context prepended to the prompt and then clamped to W'); Keystone §5.4 Result 1; Abstract.
findings.issue: a2_clamp is constructed to fail rather than representing the best achievable in-prompt delivery under the same 768-token budget. The design prepends the cross-file context to the front of the prompt and then truncates to 'last W tokens (cursor-adjacent code retained; earlier content evicted first)' — which guarantees the prepended content is evicted whenever the file is long, since eviction always removes the head first regardless of what's there. The episodic adapter's own conditioning surface is only 124 tokens on average (median 52) — trivially small relative to the 768-token budget. Nothing in the four-arm design tests the obvious honest alternative: place that same compact, symbol-specific definition near the cursor (tail of the truncated window) rather than prepending the (apparently much larger, ~12.8k-token-average) full cross-file content at the head. This is a self-contained construction flaw in the experimental design, independent of any external literature: the paper's own reported numbers show the adapter's conditioning text is small enough to fit in the budget without eviction, so a prompt-based arm using an equivalently-sized, cursor-adjacent pointer was achievable and simply was not run.
findings.why_it_matters: The entire keystone claim ('16.7x fewer prompt tokens at parity recovery', 'the adapter matches full-context prompting') is a three-way comparison between floor, a2_clamp, and episodic — and its persuasive force rests on a2_clamp being the best an engineer could do with a prompt-only channel under the same budget. It isn't: a practitioner who knows the target symbol can trivially fit a ~50-124 token pointer to it near the cursor within a 768-token window without evicting anything. If that arm were run, its recovery could plausibly approach or exceed a2_clamp's 0.183 by a wide margin, since it is functionally almost identical to the adapter's own conditioning surface just delivered through the prompt instead of through weights — collapsing much of the reported 3.4x/16.7x advantage. As constructed, the experiment demonstrates 'a full multi-thousand-token cross-file dump, prepended, is a bad way to use a 768-token budget' — which is true but not equivalent to 'the adapter beats the best achievable in-prompt channel.'
findings.fix: Add an a2_pointer (or a2_tail) arm: place the identical episodic conditioning text (the same ~124-token symbol+definition string given to the hypernetwork) at the tail of the prompt, immediately before the cursor, within the same W=768 budget — no eviction needed since it is far smaller than the budget. Report recovery for that arm alongside a2_clamp. If the adapter's advantage survives against this comparator, the keystone claim is much stronger; if it collapses, the paper needs to reframe the claim as 'weight-space delivery removes the need to identify what to place near the cursor' rather than 'weight-space delivery beats prompt delivery under a budget.'

findings.location: Abstract, second-to-last sentence ('The binding constraint is the training objective... a guarded matched-recall objective produces generalising held-out recall where a contrastive objective only suppresses alternatives'); cf. §4.2 (sec:obj) and the \todo at the end of that subsection.
findings.issue: The abstract states the objective contrast as an established, unhedged fact. The body is more careful and reveals the supporting statistics are marginal and not yet de-biased: c3 was picked as the best of a 4-point grid (c1-c4) via winner's-curse-prone selection, its own reported CI [+0.033, +0.182] is computed on the same selection data (the promised 'fresh-pool re-estimate' is an open \todo in the submitted tex), and the across-task sign test that would show the improvement is broadly distributed rather than concentrated in a few tasks lands at p=0.064 (I recompute this exactly: binomtest(17,24,0.5,two-sided) = 0.0639), i.e., not significant at conventional thresholds. 'Produces generalising held-out recall' is a stronger claim than what a marginal, selection-biased sign test supports.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader who reads only the abstract — the majority of a NeurIPS/TMLR skim — comes away believing the objective-choice finding is settled. It is directionally suggestive but explicitly flagged by the authors themselves (correctly, in the body) as unresolved pending a fresh-pool re-estimate. This is exactly the kind of abstract/body mismatch that reviewers penalize: the careful hedging work the authors did in §4.2 and §6.2 is undone by the abstract's flat phrasing.
findings.fix: Either (a) run the committed fresh-pool re-estimate before submission and report the de-biased number in the abstract, or (b) soften the abstract clause to something like 'a guarded matched-recall objective shows more consistent (though not yet fully de-biased) held-out gains than a contrastive objective, which mainly suppresses alternatives' — matching the hedged framing already present in §4.2.

findings.location: §5.4 Result 2 (Table `tab:result2`) vs. Abstract / §5.4 Result 1 ('at parity with the unbudgeted full-context ceiling (0.567)').
findings.issue: a2_full is only defined on 30/60 problems (the 8k stratum only) and is undefined at 32k by construction. The 'parity with the ceiling' headline compares the POOLED episodic recovery across both strata (31/60=0.517, dragged down by the harder 32k stratum where episodic=0.433) against a2_full measured ONLY in the easier 8k stratum (17/30=0.567). This is a population mismatch: the two numbers being called 'at parity' are not computed on the same population. When restricted to the only stratum where a2_full is actually defined, the adapter (0.600) already exceeds the ceiling (0.567), which the paper itself notes ('At 8k the adapter already meets or exceeds the full-context ceiling') but does not carry through to the headline framing.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Parity' is a weaker, muddier framing of a result that — properly stratum-matched — is actually a clean win for the adapter (0.600 vs 0.567 at 8k, the only place the ceiling is measurable). The pooled comparison instead invites the reader to average across an in-domain population (8k) and an out-of-domain population (32k, where a2_full simply has no answer), producing a number (0.517) that looks like a tie with the ceiling almost by construction — because most of the discrepancy between 0.517 and 0.567 is coming from the 32k problems where there IS no ceiling to compare against. The framing understates the strength of the 8k result and overstates what the pooled 'parity' figure actually establishes about ceiling-matching.
findings.fix: Report ceiling comparisons stratum-matched only (8k: adapter 0.600 vs. ceiling 0.567 — adapter wins, overlapping CIs) and describe the 32k stratum separately as 'ceiling not measurable; adapter recovers 0.433 where no comparator exists' rather than folding both into one pooled 'parity with ceiling' number in the abstract and Result 1.

findings.location: §4.2 (sec:obj), Table `tab:obj`, and the \todo at line ~31835 ('re-estimate +0.105 on a fresh held-out pool to de-bias selection and tighten the sign test (p=0.064)').
findings.issue: The held-out validation of the episodic conditioning surface itself (4/10 vs. floor 1/10, cited in §4.4/§5.5 as evidence the reported N=60 rows 'were never tuned on') is underpowered to the point of being uninformative on its own: Fisher's exact test on [[4,6],[1,9]] gives p=0.30; a two-proportion z-test gives p=0.12. Neither rejects the null that 4/10 and 1/10 come from the same underlying rate. The paper is right that the N=60 confirmation run is the load-bearing evidence, but it describes the n=10 pre-registration step as having 'validated' the configuration, which overstates what a non-significant n=10 check can establish on its own.
findings.why_it_matters: The paper leans on the n=10 pre-check to argue the N=60 confirmation wasn't itself the tuning set (a legitimate and important point about not tuning on the test set). But calling the n=10 step a 'validation' implies it provided independent statistical confirmation, when at n=10 it could not have rejected even a null hypothesis of no effect. The real protection against overfitting here is procedural (disjoint splits), not statistical (the n=10 check itself has no power) — the paper should say so plainly rather than let 'validated' do work the numbers don't support.
findings.fix: Reword 'validated on a disjoint held-out split (4/10 vs. floor 1/10)' to something like 'checked (non-significantly, n=10 is underpowered) on a disjoint held-out split before locking the configuration for the N=60 confirmation' — and land the promised fresh-pool re-estimate before camera-ready, since the \todo marker indicates it has not yet been run.

findings.location: Abstract, final two sentences ('the engine is a strict superset of the base on LiveCodeBench-v6 (16/63 versus 12/63, +4, zero regressions)...'); §5.5 (sec:e2e); §6.2 Limitations.
findings.issue: 'Strict superset' / 'zero regressions' is structurally guaranteed by the escalate design relative to the raw single-shot base (the base's zero-shot answer is kept if it passes; the adapter only engages on repair, so a task the base solved zero-shot cannot become a failure by construction) — it is a property of the scaffold's control flow, not empirical evidence that the adapter is beneficial. The paper's own attribution control (scale0 vs. c3) shows the adapter genuinely churns outcomes — 4 gains and 2 losses relative to the no-adapter scaffold — and the overall paired McNemar test is n.s. (p=0.125, N=63, explicitly called underpowered by the authors). The abstract nonetheless leads with the 'zero regressions' framing without flagging that this specific comparison (vs. raw base) is guaranteed by the escalation architecture rather than being a finding about the adapter's value; review_response_v10 (W1) had committed to exactly this framing fix ('"zero regressions" labelled a design property, not evidence') but I do not find that framing stated explicitly anywhere in v13.
findings.why_it_matters: A reader unfamiliar with the escalate control flow could reasonably interpret 'strict superset, zero regressions' as an empirical finding about how good the adapter is, when the real (and much weaker) empirical finding is buried two sentences later: a noisy, non-significant net +2 with real churn when the adapter is isolated from the scaffold. This is precisely the kind of gap between what's technically true and what a reader will infer that a careful reviewer should flag, and it is a committed but apparently unexecuted fix from the prior review round.
findings.fix: Add one clause at first mention of 'strict superset / zero regressions' (in the abstract, not only in the body) making explicit that this specific guarantee follows from the escalate-then-repair control flow versus the raw base, and that the adapter's own marginal contribution (scale0→c3) is small, noisy, and not significant at N=63 (p=0.125).

findings.location: §4.1 Setup and Table `tab:arms`; contrast with §4.4 Result 3 numbers for conditioning-surface size (124 tokens, median 52).
findings.issue: The exact content prepended in a2_clamp/a2_full is never precisely specified — is it the full source file(s) containing the cross-file definition, a retrieved snippet, or something intermediate? The ~12,836-token average (vs. ~13k rounded elsewhere, a minor internal inconsistency) suggests something close to full-file/full-context content, which is a very different object from the 124-token episodic pointer the adapter receives. Precisely specifying this (and why it isn't reduced to a comparably compact retrieved snippet) is necessary for a reader to judge whether a2_clamp represents 'the same information delivered through a different channel' or 'much more information than the adapter gets, delivered inefficiently.'
findings.why_it_matters: Without this detail, it's not possible to fully audit whether the four-arm design is truly an apples-to-apples channel comparison (same information, different delivery mechanism) as claimed, or whether the prompt arms are handicapped by carrying substantially more (and less filtered) content than the adapter's conditioning surface ever sees.
findings.fix: State explicitly what a2_clamp/a2_full prepend (full concatenated cross-file source vs. a filtered snippet), and reconcile the '12,836' vs. '~13k' figures to one consistent number throughout.

findings.location: §4.4 (sec:format) naive multi-file dump control; contrast with C1 above.
findings.issue: The dump-vs-episodic ablation is a valuable and correctly-run control for conditioning FORMAT (it rules out 'any adapter conditioning helps'), but it does not by itself rule out a generic-output-bias / frequency confound for the keystone metric — i.e., that identifier recovery could be inflated if the conditioned symbol happens to be a common/high-prior identifier the base model already favors, independent of genuinely reading the definition. The paper's mutated-spec control addresses this concern for the MBPP spec-absent-recall number (finding 9/19 memorization) but no analogous swapped-symbol or mismatched-conditioning control is run on the RepoBench keystone itself.
findings.why_it_matters: Given the paper's own finding that spec-absent 'recall' is substantially memorization/pointer-based elsewhere in the same system, a reviewer will reasonably ask whether the keystone's identifier recovery could similarly be partly explained by the adapter learning 'emit whatever symbol this task's ID points to' from training rather than genuinely surfacing the definition content. The naive-dump null is suggestive against this (it shows format matters) but is not a direct test of it.
findings.fix: Add a conditioning-swap control on a subset of the RepoBench keystone tasks: condition the adapter on the WRONG task's symbol/definition (from a different, non-matching problem) and check that recovery of the correct symbol drops to floor level. This would directly rule out the generic-output-bias explanation for the 0.517 keystone number specifically, rather than relying on the MBPP mutated-spec control (a different task) as indirect reassurance.

findings.location: Full document — three unresolved \todo markers (line ~18273: LSTM/vanilla-transformer encoder ablation; ~31835: fresh-pool re-estimate of +0.105; ~57130: publish SHA-256 hashes for checkpoints/corpus).
findings.issue: Three visible red \todo placeholders remain in the submitted v13 tex, all corresponding to author actions explicitly committed in review_response_v10 ('Fresh held-out pool for c3', 'Publish grade JSONs, full sha256s, c3 checkpoint'). These are not cosmetic — the fresh-pool re-estimate is the action that would resolve finding C2/C4 above, and the hash publication is what would let a reviewer actually verify reproducibility claims in Appendix A.
findings.why_it_matters: Submitting with unresolved \todo markers signals the committed revision plan from the prior review round is incomplete, which will read to a reviewer as either an oversight or an implicit admission that the de-biased number wasn't obtained (perhaps because it changed the result unfavorably).
findings.fix: Either complete the three committed actions before this submission round, or — if truly out of scope for this version — remove the visible \todo markup and state the limitation in prose in §6.2 instead of leaving a to-do artifact in camera-facing text.

findings.location: Contributions paragraph (~1600 chars in, 'roughly 13k tokens') vs. §5.4 Result 1 ('averaging 12,836 tokens').
findings.issue: Minor inconsistency in reporting the average full-context prompt length (rounded '~13k' vs. exact '12,836').
findings.why_it_matters: Trivial, but small inconsistencies in reported numbers invite a reviewer to wonder whether other reported figures were computed from the same run or drift across recomputations.
findings.fix: Use one figure consistently, or explicitly note the rounding.

findings.location: §5.4 Result 2 / Abstract ('At a 32k context the in-prompt arm is infeasible on every problem').
findings.issue: 'At a 32k context the in-prompt arm is infeasible on every problem' could be read as a hard model limitation, but per latest_benchmarks.md the actual constraint is a self-imposed 12k-token grading budget in the harness, not a fundamental incapacity of the base model to ingest 32k tokens. Note: the paper itself never states Qwen3-4B-Instruct's numeric context window (I searched paper_v13.tex for '262k'/'262,144'/'262144' and found zero occurrences there — that figure appears only in latest_benchmarks.md, a supporting doc, not the paper). The paper's only related-work mention of context sizes is a generic list of scaling approaches ('4K, 32K, 128K, sometimes 1M'), not a claim about this specific model. So the paper does not currently ground why a2_full is 'infeasible' at 32k in a stated model capability at all.
findings.why_it_matters: Without the paper itself stating the base model's actual context window, a reader has no way to judge whether the 32k in-prompt arm is 'infeasible' because of a genuine base-model limit or purely because of an evaluation-harness choice (the 12k-token grading budget mentioned in the supporting benchmarks doc). The paper should state this explicitly rather than leaving it implicit or only documented outside the manuscript.
findings.fix: State explicitly in the paper (not just the supporting benchmarks doc) what governs the 32k 'infeasible' claim — i.e., name the grading/context budget used by the harness and confirm whether it reflects a genuine base-model context limit or an evaluation-design choice.

verdict: Novelty and citation integrity are, on the whole, a strength of this paper rather than a liability. I independently verified all 14 of the flagged 2025-2026 references via arXiv and OpenAlex: every one resolves to a real paper with matching title, first author, and ID (Doc-to-LoRA 2602.15902, SHINE 2602.06358, TC-LoRA 2510.09561, Ouroboros 2604.02051, ReasonCACHE 2602.02366, Transformer-Squared 2501.06252, pink2025 2502.06975, SICA 2504.15228, ACE 2510.04618, tandon TTT 2512.23675, gozeten TTT 2503.11842, hu TTL 2505.20633, T2L 2506.06105, shi 2509.23040). None are fabricated. The narrow novelty claim -- 'per-step conditioning of the adapter on an agent's reasoning trajectory' -- is honestly scoped and survives an active search for collapsing prior art: the nearest neighbors that surface are exactly the works the paper already cites, and its differentiations from each (TC-LoRA = diffusion-timestep, Doc-to-LoRA/SHINE/T2L = once-per-doc, Ouroboros = hidden-state modulation over frozen SVD bases) are accurate against the source abstracts. I also fetched and checked the two named attributions directly: Transformer^2 (2501.06252) mixes RL-trained SVD 'expert' vectors via a per-prompt two-pass dispatch and does not read trajectory state, so the paper's characterization is accurate; and Schuurmans (2301.04589) proves a transformer with an external read-write memory is computationally universal 'without any modification of the language model weights,' which the paper cites correctly (weight updates are not necessary for universal computation). The primary Liu2022 PEFT-vs-ICL attribution is correct. The one substantive weakness on this track is the treatment of ReasonCACHE: the paper cites it as a competitive KV-cache alternative that 'matches or exceeds LoRA-based updates,' frames the token-vs-weight question as 'empirical' that it 'tests directly,' and then tests only adapter-vs-in-prompt-clamp -- never against the KV/prefix channel that ReasonCACHE occupies and that its abstract proves dominates low-rank weight updates in expressivity. Secondary issues are the imprecise 'third axis' framing, a slanted Liu2022 citation in the boundary section, unverifiable/forward-dated conference venue tags in the bib, and one wrong first-author name. No blocking or novelty-collapsing problems for this track.

findings.location: Related Work, 'Self-improving agents and the in-context/PEFT trade-off' paragraph; and Sec. 5.4 keystone framing
findings.issue: ReasonCACHE (gupta2026reasoncache, verified 2602.02366) is cited as a KV-cache method that 'injects the context into the KV cache and matches or exceeds LoRA-based updates on several reasoning benchmarks without touching parameters,' immediately followed by 'Which channel wins is empirical... We test that boundary directly.' But the keystone experiment tests only adapter (episodic) vs. in-prompt context (a2_clamp/a2_full) vs. no-context floor. It never runs ReasonCACHE or any KV-cache/prefix-tuning arm. Worse, ReasonCACHE's abstract explicitly proves it 'can be strictly more expressive than low-rank weight update since the latter ties expressivity to input rank' -- a direct theoretical challenge to the paper's core mechanism (a low-rank LoRA delta) that the paper cites but does not engage. So the paper names the single most central comparator, asserts the question is empirical, claims to test it, and then omits the comparator.
findings.why_it_matters: ReasonCACHE lives in exactly the paper's motivating regime (reasoning beyond the context window, no base-weight update, addressing the O(t^2) attention cost) and is the natural head-to-head. A reviewer will read 'we test that boundary directly' as a promise to compare against the cited competitive channel, not merely against a naive in-prompt clamp that is the weakest possible alternative. Beating an evict-first in-prompt baseline is a much weaker result than beating a KV-cache method that claims theoretical expressivity dominance over LoRA. This is the sharpest instance of the prior review's W2 (missing PEFT/KV comparator) and the one most likely to be demanded in rebuttal.
findings.fix: Either (a) add a ReasonCACHE / prefix-tuning / KV-injection arm under the same W=768 budget on RepoBench cross_file_first, or (b) soften the framing: drop 'we test that boundary directly,' state that the keystone compares the adapter against the in-prompt channel only, and explicitly list KV-cache/prefix methods (ReasonCACHE) as an unrun comparator alongside the already-conceded Gate-1 direct-PEFT arm. Also engage ReasonCACHE's rank-tied-expressivity argument in Related Work rather than citing it only as supporting evidence.

findings.location: Title and Introduction ('third axis'); Intro para 1 (context-scaling / RAG framing)
findings.issue: The 'third memory axis' framing rests on a trichotomy -- context-window scaling, RAG, weight-memory -- but by the paper's own description RAG merely 'decides which earlier tokens to fetch back into the same window,' i.e. it operates in the same token/attention substrate as context scaling. Those are one axis (token memory), not two. Meanwhile the framing omits the KV-cache / prefix-tuning / soft-prompt family that sits between token memory and weight memory -- precisely where ReasonCACHE (cited by the paper) positions itself as 'a middle path between in-context and in-weight learning.' So weight-memory is one point in a populated space, not a clean orthogonal third axis, and the space is mis-partitioned.
findings.why_it_matters: 'Third axis' is the paper's headline positioning claim. A reviewer who notices that two of the three axes share a substrate, and that a whole intermediate family (which the paper itself cites) is missing from the taxonomy, will read the framing as marketing rather than a principled decomposition. The technical contribution does not need the trichotomy to stand.
findings.fix: Recast as token-memory (context window + RAG as one substrate) vs. KV/activation memory (prefix/KV-cache) vs. weight memory, and position the contribution within that fuller space; or drop the 'third axis' language and frame weight-space episodic memory as a complementary substrate rather than a numbered new axis.

findings.location: Sec. 5.3 (in-context boundary): 'in-context learning is strong precisely when the full context fits and is read once~\citep{liu2022fewshot}'
findings.issue: liu2022fewshot ('Few-Shot Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning is Better and Cheaper than In-Context Learning', NeurIPS 2022, verified) is an anti-ICL result: its thesis is that PEFT beats ICL in both accuracy and per-query cost. Citing it to support the pro-ICL near-field claim ('ICL is strong when the context fits and is read once') uses the paper against its grain. The Related Work citation of the same paper ('few-shot PEFT can match or beat in-context learning at lower per-query cost once trained') is accurate; only the Sec. 5.3 usage is slanted.
findings.why_it_matters: A reviewer familiar with T-Few/IA3 will flag a citation deployed to support the opposite of the cited paper's finding. It is a small credibility ding in a section where the paper is otherwise commendably candid about the prompt winning.
findings.fix: Cite a source that actually supports 'ICL is strong when the full context fits' (e.g. an ICL capability result), or reword to note that even Liu2022's PEFT-favouring result concedes ICL is competitive in the read-once, in-window regime -- without implying Liu2022 endorses ICL superiority there.

findings.location: refs.bib: charakorn2025t2l (@inproceedings ICML 2025), gozeten2025ttt (ICML 2025), hu2025ttl (ICML 2025), zhang2025ace (@inproceedings ICLR 2026)
findings.issue: Four references are typed as peer-reviewed conference papers, but the venue attributions cannot be independently confirmed (OpenAlex resolves each only to its arXiv/preprint record) and one is forward-dated: zhang2025ace (ACE, arXiv 2510.04618, submitted Oct 2025) is listed as ICLR 2026 @inproceedings, a venue whose decisions would not have been final when this manuscript was prepared. By contrast, cho2025tclora's NeurIPS-2025-SpaVLE-Workshop tag IS corroborated by the arXiv comment field, and liu2024repobench (ICLR 2024) and liu2022fewshot (NeurIPS 2022) are genuine -- so the problem is specific to the four above, not systemic.
findings.why_it_matters: Premature or unverifiable @inproceedings tags are a common camera-ready error that reviewers and area chairs do check. Claiming an ICLR 2026 acceptance for a recent preprint that may still be under review is the kind of bibliographic overstatement that erodes trust, even when the paper itself exists.
findings.fix: Downgrade unconfirmed entries to @misc/@article with the arXiv id until acceptance is verifiable; keep the conference tag only where corroborated (as with TC-LoRA). Re-run the 'web-verified' pass the bib header claims, this time confirming venue/year, not just existence.

findings.location: refs.bib: shi2025revisit author field ('Yu Shi and others')
findings.issue: The bib lists the first author of 'Look Back to Reason Forward: Revisitable Memory...' (2509.23040) as 'Yu Shi'; the actual arXiv first author is 'Yaorui Shi'. The bib entry itself carries the note 'co-author list not independently verified,' confirming the author list was never checked. The citation's use in Related Work ('revisitable-memory architectures... elaborate the external-store design empirically') is accurate; only the author name is wrong.
findings.why_it_matters: A wrong first-author surname in a reference list is a factual error reviewers occasionally spot-check, and a bib comment openly admitting the entry is unverified signals incomplete bibliographic diligence.
findings.fix: Correct to 'Yaorui Shi et al.' and remove the self-flagged 'not independently verified' note after confirming the full author list.

findings.location: Related Work: ReasonCACHE described as operating 'without touching parameters'
findings.issue: ReasonCACHE is an instantiation of Prefix Tuning that distills demonstrations into a fixed key-value cache; the prefix/KV is a set of trained parameters (its abstract counts 'trainable parameters' as an efficiency axis). 'Without touching parameters' conflates 'no base-weight update' with 'no trained parameters at all.' The intended meaning (base model unchanged) is correct, but the phrasing overstates.
findings.why_it_matters: Minor precision issue; a KV/prefix-tuning-literate reviewer will note that prefix tuning does learn parameters, and imprecision here slightly undercuts the point in NOV-1 that the paper should engage ReasonCACHE carefully.
findings.fix: Reword to 'without updating the base model's weights' or 'without in-weight learning of the backbone,' matching ReasonCACHE's own 'middle path between in-context and in-weight learning' characterization.

verdict: The manuscript is in strong internal shape on the dimension that most often sinks a resubmission: the keystone numbers are consistent across abstract, intro, results, and discussion. I cross-checked 0.517 / 0.150 / 0.183 / 0.567 / 0.433, 16.7x, the HumanEval+ 134/135 superset, 16/63 vs 12/63 (+4) with the +2/+2 scaffold/adapter split, +0.105 (CI, 17/24, sign p=0.064), the 124/median-52 conditioning, and the scaling multipliers (0.627x MBPP, 0.91x RepoBench, lora_alpha 45.25) across every occurrence — all agree, and the stale abstract LCB numbers the brief worried about (12/49 vs 9/49) are gone. Citations are clean (25 used = 25 defined, no orphans/dangling). The blocking problem is not a number: it is submission format. The class is tmlr[preprint] rendering non-anonymized authors, yet the folder is 'NeuroIPS Submission', a neurips_2026.sty sits beside tmlr.sty, the title declares no venue, and the compiled PDF is 15 pages — the author has not committed to a venue, and every candidate resolution changes the required format (TMLR review is double-blind, so [preprint]+real-names is wrong; NeurIPS 2026 is a different class, double-blind, and a 9-page main-text limit that 15 pages violates). That must be resolved before submission. Below that: one genuine internal-naming collision ('functional-49' names both the benchmark and a 49-item subset of the 63-item set); three open \todo items, two of which (SHA-256 hashes, fresh-pool re-estimate of the selection-biased +0.105) are camera-ready-blocking; and a keystone-framing subtlety where the 16.7x 'parity' pairs a two-stratum episodic number against a one-stratum ceiling while the cleaner within-8k comparison that the adapter actually wins is buried in Table 5. Prose is precise and disciplined but leans hard on one rhetorical device (29 comma-antithesis ', not Y' constructions, 14 'rather than', 5 'In practice') and the abstract is a single 432-word, 14-sentence block. None of the prose issues are blocking; the venue and the two hash/re-estimate todos are.

findings.location: \documentclass line (\usepackage[preprint]{tmlr}), \title, \author block; folder 'NeuroIPS Submission'; drafts/ contains both tmlr.sty and neurips_2026.sty; compiled PDF = 15 pp
findings.issue: The venue is undecided and the current format is internally contradictory. The class is TMLR in [preprint] mode, which renders full author names and affiliations (Dolev, Kachman, Gendre + emails). But the containing folder is 'NeuroIPS Submission', a neurips_2026.sty is staged beside tmlr.sty, and the title states no venue. Each plausible target implies a different, currently-unmet format: (a) TMLR review is double-blind on OpenReview — a real-submission build should use the anonymized submission mode, not [preprint] with author names; (b) NeurIPS 2026 would require the NeurIPS class (not tmlr), is double-blind, and enforces a ~9-page main-text limit that the 15-page PDF exceeds by a wide margin.
findings.why_it_matters: A venue/anonymization/length mismatch is a desk-reject risk that fires before any reviewer reads the science. Submitting a non-anonymized [preprint] build to a double-blind track, or a 15-page paper under a 9-page limit, can end the review before it starts — independent of how strong the results are.
findings.fix: Decide the venue explicitly and build for it. If TMLR: switch to the anonymized submission mode (drop [preprint]/real names for the review build), keep the 15 pp (TMLR has no page limit), and delete neurips_2026.sty from the tree. If NeurIPS 2026: swap to the NeurIPS 2026 class, cut main text to the page limit (move material to the appendix), keep it anonymized, and delete tmlr.sty. Rename the folder to match once decided so it stops signalling the wrong target.

findings.location: §5.1 Setup, Benchmarks ('LiveCodeBench~v6 functional-49') vs §5.6 e2e ('full functional set, N=63'; '(The functional-49 subset alone gives base 9 / scale0 11 / c3 12)'); Table 5 (tab:lcb) caption 'full functional set, N=63'
findings.issue: The token 'functional-49' is used for two different objects. In Setup it names THE post-cutoff end-to-end benchmark ('LiveCodeBench~v6 functional-49 is the post-cutoff end-to-end check'). In §5.6 the end-to-end benchmark is 'the full functional set, N=63', and 'functional-49' is demoted to a 49-item SUBSET of that 63-item set. A reader cannot reconcile 'functional-49' (the named benchmark, Setup) with 'N=63 full functional set' (the reported benchmark, e2e).
findings.why_it_matters: This is the one genuine internal-naming inconsistency in the paper, and it sits on the headline end-to-end result (16/63, +4). A reviewer parsing Setup will expect N=49 in the LCB table and instead find N=63, then hit a parenthetical calling functional-49 a subset — reading as either a stale number or a moved goalpost, exactly the impression the +4/-0 result can least afford.
findings.fix: Pick one canonical name. In Setup, describe the benchmark as 'LiveCodeBench-v6, full post-cutoff functional set (N=63)' and, if the 49-item subset is worth mentioning, introduce it there explicitly as 'the functional-49 subset (N=49) used in prior versions'. Ensure Setup, §5.6, Table 5, and the appendix all use N=63 as the primary set and never use 'functional-49' as the benchmark's name.

findings.location: \todo macros at §3.2 (arch: 'add LSTM and vanilla-transformer encoder ablations'), §5.2 (obj: 're-estimate +0.105 on a fresh held-out pool ... tighten the sign test p=0.064'), Appendix A ('publish SHA-256 hashes for checkpoints and corpus splits')
findings.issue: Three \todo{} placeholders remain, and they are not equal in urgency. (i) SHA-256 hashes: the Reproducibility appendix explicitly promises them and they are absent — the repro claim is currently uncheckable, and this was a committed author action from the v10 review (item 4). (ii) Fresh-pool re-estimate of +0.105: the point estimate is acknowledged as selection-biased (c3 chosen from the grid) and the across-task sign test is borderline (p=0.064); the paper itself flags this as required to de-bias. (iii) LSTM/vanilla-transformer encoder ablations: the paper's Perceiver-vs-mean-pool argument (§3.2) currently rests on a single alternative (mean-pool), so the 'the architecture is not what gates this' framing is only partially supported on the encoder axis.
findings.why_it_matters: \todo macros are rendered in red bold in the PDF and cannot ship in a camera-ready. Beyond cosmetics: the missing hashes make the reproducibility appendix a promissory note, and the un-debiased +0.105 with p=0.064 means the §5.2 'objective is the binding constraint' claim rests on a selected point estimate whose significance is not yet established.
findings.fix: Before camera-ready: (a) compute and publish the SHA-256 hashes — mechanical, do it now and strip the todo; (b) run the fresh-pool re-estimate and report the de-biased +0.105 with the recomputed sign test, or explicitly downgrade the §5.2 claim to 'suggestive on a selected configuration' if the sign test stays >0.05; (c) either run the LSTM/transformer encoder ablations or narrow the §3.2 claim to 'Perceiver beats mean-pool' rather than implying a general encoder-architecture insensitivity. For a submission (pre-camera-ready) build, at minimum convert (a) to a done item and reword (b)/(c) so no red todo renders.

findings.location: Abstract; §1 intro; §5.4 Result 1 (tab:result1) vs §5.4 Result 2 (tab:result2); '16.7x ... at parity recovery', '0.517 vs a2_full 0.567', '12,836 tokens'
findings.issue: The headline 'parity at 16.7x' pairs mismatched strata. episodic 0.517 is computed over the full N=60 (8k+32k), but the a2_full ceiling 0.567 is 17/30 — defined only on the 8k stratum (a2_full is undefined at 32k). So '0.517 at parity with 0.567' compares a two-stratum (harder, mixed) episodic number against an easy-stratum-only ceiling. The apples-to-apples within-8k comparison in Table 5 (tab:result2) is episodic 0.600 vs a2_full 0.567 — where the adapter actually EXCEEDS the ceiling — and it is buried below the headline. Separately, the 12,836-token average that yields 16.7x has no stated basis: is it averaged over the 30 problems where a2_full is defined (8k), or over all 60? If it is the 8k-stratum average, then the ratio's numerator and the episodic 0.517 in the same sentence are drawn from different problem sets.
findings.why_it_matters: The paper's most-quoted claim (parity at 16.7x fewer tokens) is, as framed, conservative in a way that also conceals its own stronger, cleaner result, and rests on a denominator whose problem-set basis is unspecified. A careful reviewer will notice that the 0.517-vs-0.567 pair mixes strata and will ask what set 12,836 averages over; leaving it implicit invites a 'the comparison is not matched' objection on the keystone.
findings.fix: State the basis of 12,836 explicitly (which arm, which strata, N). Lead the parity claim with the matched within-8k comparison (episodic 0.600 vs ceiling 0.567 on the same 30 problems) since it is both fair and stronger, then report the pooled 0.517 as the conservative all-strata figure with the 32k caveat. If 12,836 is the 8k-stratum average, say so and pair 16.7x with the 8k episodic 0.600, not the pooled 0.517.

findings.location: Abstract ('26.8x prompt-length reduction'); §1 intro; §5.4 Result 2 ('Against the 32k context the prompt-length reduction is 26.8x')
findings.issue: The 26.8x figure is asserted with no stated denominator and is not a parity comparison. Unlike 16.7x (which cites the 12,836-token average), 26.8x has no accompanying token count anywhere. And at 32k the a2_full ceiling is 'undefined (prohibitive, 30/30)' — it recovers nothing — so there is no recovery-matched arm to be '26.8x shorter than at parity'. 26.8x can only be a raw ratio of some (unstated) 32k context length to 768, against an arm that produced no answer.
findings.why_it_matters: Presenting 26.8x in the same breath as the 16.7x 'parity' ratio implies it is the same kind of quantity (a parity-matched token reduction). It is not: there is no parity at 32k because the comparator is undefined. An unstated denominator on a headline multiplier is exactly the kind of number a reviewer will demand to see derived.
findings.fix: State the 32k-stratum average full-context token count that produces 26.8x (e.g. '~20.6k tokens / 768'), and reword to make clear it is a raw prompt-length ratio against an infeasible in-prompt arm, not a parity-matched reduction: 'at 32k the in-prompt arm cannot run at all; the adapter holds a 768-token prompt against a ~X-token context, a 26.8x reduction, while still recovering 0.433.'

findings.location: Abstract (\begin{abstract} ... \end{abstract})
findings.issue: The abstract is a single unbroken paragraph of ~432 words / ~14 sentences that carries the full mechanism, the four-arm design, three secondary findings, two caveats, and the end-to-end results. It opens mid-mechanism ('At every reasoning step, a hypernetwork H_theta reads the running trajectory...') before the reader knows what problem is being solved.
findings.why_it_matters: A 432-word single block is hard to scan and buries the keystone in the middle; area chairs and reviewers triage on the abstract. The density works against the paper's own stated 'idea-first, no hype' discipline by front-loading notation before motivation.
findings.fix: Tighten to ~200-250 words and either split into two short paragraphs (problem+mechanism / results+bound) or lead with the one-sentence problem framing ('On the edge, the context window is the binding constraint...') before the H_theta machinery. Move the HumanEval+ and scaffold-split detail to the intro; keep the abstract to mechanism, keystone (0.517 vs 0.150/0.183, parity at 16.7x, the identifier-recovery bound), and one caveat.

findings.location: Throughout body (abstract→conclusion): 29 comma-antithesis ', not Y' constructions, 14 'rather than', 5 'In practice', ~60 em-dashes
findings.issue: The prose leans heavily on one rhetorical figure — the 'X, not Y' / 'A, not B' antithesis — used 29 times, plus 14 'rather than' and 5 paragraph-closing 'In practice' transitions. Examples cluster: 'a memory-architecture question, not an alignment or a scale one'; 'the constant object is the prompt; the total work is not'; 'identifier recovery, not functional pass@1'; 'as the scope of the definition, not as a roadmap'. Several 'In practice' sentences are hollow restatements of the preceding result ('In practice, the model gets the out-of-file API it needs without paying for it in context it does not have').
findings.why_it_matters: Used once or twice the antithesis is crisp; at 29 occurrences plus the repeated 'In practice' closer it reads as a mannerism and is a recognizable AI-writing tell that reviewers increasingly flag. The hollow 'In practice' transitions add words without adding information, cutting against the stated no-hype discipline.
findings.fix: Keep the antithesis where the contrast is load-bearing (e.g. 'identifier recovery, not pass@1' — that one earns its place) and rewrite ~half of the others as plain declaratives. Delete or fold the 5 'In practice' closers into the sentence that precedes them; if the point is already made, cut it.

findings.location: §3.3, Algorithm 1 (the \fbox{\begin{minipage}...} block); references 'Algorithm~1' in §1, §3.3
findings.issue: Algorithm 1 is typeset as a hand-built fbox+minipage, not a floating numbered environment (no \begin{algorithm}, no \label, the number '1' is hardcoded in the text). All cross-references write the literal 'Algorithm~1'.
findings.why_it_matters: The number is not tracked by LaTeX: adding a second algorithm, or any reordering, silently breaks the numbering and every hardcoded 'Algorithm~1' reference. It also will not appear in a list-of-algorithms and cannot be \ref'd.
findings.fix: Wrap it in a proper float (algorithm2e or the algorithm/algorithmic packages) with a \caption and \label{alg:loop}, and replace hardcoded 'Algorithm~1' with '\ref{alg:loop}'. Low effort, removes a fragility. If keeping the fbox for stylistic reasons, at least define a counter so the number is not literal.

findings.location: figures/ and drafts/ both contain figure2.pdf AND figure2_repobench.pdf; \includegraphics{figure2_repobench.pdf} in §5.4; Fig. 1 = figure1.pdf
findings.issue: The paper includes figure2_repobench.pdf (the correct four-arm RepoBench bar chart) — so the right file is referenced. But a stale figure2.pdf also sits in both figures/ and drafts/ and is not referenced anywhere in the .tex. I was unable to obtain a rendered visual read on the figure content in this session, so I cannot certify legibility, axis labels, CI whisker rendering, or colour-thread consistency with the text; that verification is still owed. There is no figure showing recovery as a function of prompt budget W.
findings.why_it_matters: An unreferenced stale figure2.pdf in the tree invites the wrong file being picked up on a clean rebuild or by a co-author, and it is the exact ambiguity the brief flagged. And the keystone's core message ('the advantage grows as the budget tightens / the context grows') is currently carried only by two static bar tables (Tables 4-5); a recovery-vs-budget curve would show the crossover directly.
findings.fix: Delete or archive the unreferenced figure2.pdf so only figure2_repobench.pdf remains, and confirm the \includegraphics path resolves to it on a clean build. Author must eyeball the compiled Fig. 2 for legibility at print size (axis labels, four-arm labels, Wilson whiskers, arm colours matching the text). Consider adding a panel plotting identifier recovery vs prompt budget W (and/or vs context-length stratum) for episodic vs a2_clamp — it would make the 'largest exactly where the prompt cannot hold the context' claim visual rather than tabular.

findings.location: §5.6 (LCB), §6.3 limitations ('not the pre-registered Gate 1 test, which requires a direct-PEFT comparator'); refs.bib
findings.issue: The v10 adversarial-review dispositions committed to adding several citations — TMEM ('cited as the comparison standard'), Mosbach et al. 2023, Meta-Tool, Override Gap — and none of them appear in v13 (verified absent from both tex and refs.bib). The Gate-1 / direct-PEFT limitation sentence now stands without the TMEM comparison-standard citation the rebuttal promised, and the 'one family, one domain' limitation no longer cites Mosbach.
findings.why_it_matters: For a fresh submission this is low-stakes, but if any v10 reviewer sees v13, the dropped citations read as un-kept rebuttal commitments. More substantively, the 'direct-PEFT comparator still open' limitation is stronger when it names the standard (TMEM) it is measuring itself against.
findings.fix: Either re-add the TMEM citation to the Gate-1/direct-PEFT limitation and Mosbach to the single-family limitation (restoring the committed comparators), or, if they were dropped deliberately for scope, make sure nothing in the text still implies they are cited. Low priority relative to P1-P5.

findings.location: §1 intro ('a full-context prompt averaging roughly 13k tokens') vs §5.4 / tab:result1 caption ('averaging 12,836 tokens'); §6.1 discussion ('16/63 to 12/63')
findings.issue: Two harmless surface wrinkles: (a) the intro rounds the full-context average to '13k' while the results state 12,836 — acceptable rounding but worth making consistent (e.g. '~12.8k'); (b) §6.1 writes the LCB result as '16/63 to 12/63', ordering the larger number first with 'to', which reads as a decrease direction even though it means base 12 → engine 16.
findings.why_it_matters: Neither is wrong, but '13k' vs '12,836' can momentarily read as two different measurements, and '16/63 to 12/63' briefly parses backwards. Both are one-word fixes that remove reader friction.
findings.fix: Round the intro to '~12.8k tokens' (or state 12,836 in both places), and rephrase §6.1 as '12/63 to 16/63 (+4)' so the direction reads as an increase, matching the abstract's '16/63 versus 12/63'.

findings.location: \textbf{Contributions.} paragraph, §1
findings.issue: The contributions are a single ~225-word paragraph enumerating five items with inline 'First / Second / Third — the keystone — / Fourth / Fifth'. It is readable but dense, and the em-dash-flagged keystone ('Third—the keystone—') is easy to skim past inside the block.
findings.why_it_matters: A five-item contribution list buried in prose is harder to scan than a formatted list; reviewers often lift the contributions verbatim into their summary, and the keystone deserves to be visually unmissable.
findings.fix: Consider a \begin{enumerate} (or bold lead-ins per item) so each contribution is its own scannable line, and set the keystone item apart (e.g. bold 'Keystone:'). Optional — the current prose is acceptable, this is polish.
